claim: Neurotransmitter release depends on the SNARE complex formed by syntaxin-1, synaptobrevin and SNAP-25.
source: Neurotransmitter release depends on the SNARE complex formed by syntaxin-1, synaptobrevin and SNAP-25, as well as on complexins, which bind to the SNARE complex and play active and inhibitory roles.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the SNARE complex's role in neurotransmitter release.

claim: Complexins bind to the SNARE complex and play active and inhibitory roles.

claim: A crystal structure of a Complexin-I fragment bearing a 'superclamp' mutation bound to a truncated SNARE complex lacking the C-terminus of the synaptobrevin SNARE motif (SNAREΔ60) has been determined.
source: A crystal structure of a Complexin-I fragment bearing a so-called 'superclamp' mutation bound to a truncated SNARE complex lacking the C-terminus of the synaptobrevin SNARE motif (SNAREΔ60) suggested that an 'accessory' α-helix of Complexin-I inhibits release by inserting into the C-terminus of the SNARE complex.
evidence: The manuscript references a crystal structure that was previously determined.

claim: The crystal structure suggested that an 'accessory' α-helix of Complexin-I inhibits release by inserting into the C-terminus of the SNARE complex.

evidence: This is an interpretation from a previously published crystal structure.

claim: The release of neurotransmitters by Ca2+-triggered synaptic vesicle exocytosis is governed by a sophisticated protein machinery that includes the neuronal soluble N-ethylmaleimide sensitive factor attachment protein receptors (SNAREs) synaptobrevin, syntaxin-1 and SNAP-25 as central components.
source: The release of neurotransmitters by Ca2+-triggered synaptic vesicle exocytosis is governed by a sophisticated protein machinery that includes the neuronal soluble N-ethylmaleimide sensitive factor attachment protein receptors (SNAREs) synaptobrevin, syntaxin-1 and SNAP-25 as central components (Südhof and Rothman, 2009; Rizo and Xu, 2015).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The SNARE complex consists of a four-helix bundle.
source: These proteins form a tight SNARE complex that consists of a four-helix bundle and plays a key role in membrane fusion by bringing the synaptic vesicle and plasma membranes together (Söllner et al., 1993; Sutton et al., 1998; Weber et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The SNARE complex plays a key role in membrane fusion by bringing the synaptic vesicle and plasma membranes together.
source: These proteins form a tight SNARE complex that consists of a four-helix bundle and plays a key role in membrane fusion by bringing the synaptic vesicle and plasma membranes together (Söllner et al., 1993; Sutton et al., 1998; Weber et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Complexins bind tightly to the SNARE complex.
source: These small soluble proteins bind tightly to the SNARE complex (McMahon et al., 1995) and play both active and inhibitory roles in release (Reim et al., 2001; Huntwork and Littleton, 2007; Hobson et al., 2011; Martin et al., 2011), but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to McMahon et al., 1995.

claim: Complexins play both active and inhibitory roles in release.
source: These small soluble proteins bind tightly to the SNARE complex (McMahon et al., 1995) and play both active and inhibitory roles in release (Reim et al., 2001; Huntwork and Littleton, 2007; Hobson et al., 2011; Martin et al., 2011), but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The mechanisms by which complexins play active and inhibitory roles in release remain unclear.
source: These small soluble proteins bind tightly to the SNARE complex (McMahon et al., 1995) and play both active and inhibitory roles in release (Reim et al., 2001; Huntwork and Littleton, 2007; Hobson et al., 2011; Martin et al., 2011), but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: A crystal structure of the SNARE complex bound to a fragment spanning residues 26–83 of Complexin-I showed that binding involves a central α-helix of CpxI.
source: A crystal structure of the SNARE complex bound to a fragment spanning residues 26–83 of Complexin-I [CpxI(26-83)] showed that binding involves a central α-helix of CpxI, while a preceding accessory α-helix does not contact the SNAREs (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by a crystal structure shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: In the crystal structure of the SNARE complex bound to CpxI(26-83), a preceding accessory α-helix does not contact the SNAREs.
source: A crystal structure of the SNARE complex bound to a fragment spanning residues 26–83 of Complexin-I [CpxI(26-83)] showed that binding involves a central α-helix of CpxI, while a preceding accessory α-helix does not contact the SNAREs (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by a crystal structure shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Electrophysiological studies indicated that the accessory helix mediates at least in part the inhibitory role of CpxI.
source: Electrophysiological studies indicated that the accessory helix mediates at least in part the inhibitory role of CpxI, leading to a model whereby the accessory helix inhibits release by replacing part of the synaptobrevin SNARE motif in a partially assembled SNARE complex, thus preventing C-terminal assembly of the complex (Xue et al., 2007; Maximov et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to electrophysiological studies.

claim: A model proposes that the accessory helix inhibits release by replacing part of the synaptobrevin SNARE motif in a partially assembled SNARE complex, thus preventing C-terminal assembly of the complex.
source: Electrophysiological studies indicated that the accessory helix mediates at least in part the inhibitory role of CpxI, leading to a model whereby the accessory helix inhibits release by replacing part of the synaptobrevin SNARE motif in a partially assembled SNARE complex, thus preventing C-terminal assembly of the complex (Xue et al., 2007; Maximov et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a model based on electrophysiological studies cited.

claim: Cell-cell fusion assays supported the model whereby the accessory helix inhibits release by replacing part of the synaptobrevin SNARE motif.
source: Cell-cell fusion assays supported this model and led to the design of several CpxI mutants with increased or decreased inhibitory activity in these assays, including a 'superclamp' mutant where three charged residues were replaced with hydrophobic residues (D27L, E34F, R37A) to enhance the putative binding to the partially assembled SNARE complex (Giraudo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to cell-cell fusion assays.

claim: Cell-cell fusion assays led to the design of several CpxI mutants with increased or decreased inhibitory activity in these assays.

claim: A crystal structure of SNAREΔ60 bound to CpxI(26-83) bearing the superclamp mutation revealed a zig-zag array where the central helix binds to one SNAREΔ60 complex and the accessory helix binds to another SNAREΔ60 complex.
source: A crystal structure of a SNARE complex with synaptobrevin truncated at residue 60 (SNAREΔ60) bound to CpxI(26-83) bearing the superclamp mutation [scCpxI(26-83)] later revealed a zig-zag array where the central helix binds to one SNAREΔ60 complex and the accessory helix binds to another SNAREΔ60 complex (Figure 1C), suggesting that such an array inhibits neurotransmitter release before Ca2+ influx (Kümmel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a crystal structure shown in Figure 1C and cited.
